item.title: CVE-2026-42533 Exposes Critical Pre-Auth nginx RCE Flaw
item.description:
CVE-2026-42533 is a critical pre-auth nginx RCE with a 10/10 lab exploitation rate, ASLR bypass included. Patch nginx now: 1.30.4, 1.31.3, and NGINX Plus R36 P7 or 37.0.3.1 are the fixed releases.
- CVE-2026-42533 affects nginx 0.9.6 through 1.30.3 stable and 1.31.2 mainline, plus NGINX Plus R33-R36 and 37.0.0.1-37.0.2.1. No auth, no client cert, no unusual setup required. PoC exists but is being withheld. Treat this as actively exploitable in the near term.
- Root cause: nginx's two-pass evaluation engine (LEN pass then VALUE pass) does not save and restore PCRE capture state. A regex map evaluation can overwrite shared capture data mid-flight, making LEN and VALUE disagree on buffer size, producing a heap overflow or an info leak. Chaining both gives reliable RCE with ASLR defeated.
- Vulnerable pattern: any config combining regex captures ($1 or named groups) with regex map variables in the same evaluation path. Affected directives include proxy_set_header, proxy_pass, rewrite, add_header, and root, across both HTTP and stream modules.
- The researcher released a static configuration scanner to flag vulnerable patterns without exploitation. Audit configs before patching where immediate upgrades are constrained.
Upgrade to 1.30.4 or 1.31.3 immediately. Run the released config scanner to identify exposed directive chains. Confirm NGINX Plus is on R36 P7 or 37.0.3.1. Prior CVE patches do not cover this flaw.

item.title: From Web Request to Domain Compromise: Understanding the July 2026 SharePoint Attacks
item.description:
Six CVEs hit on-prem SharePoint in July 2026, four now in CISA KEV with active exploitation confirmed. Unauthenticated RCE and auth bypass can chain from a single web request to full domain compromise.
- CVE-2026-56164 (CVSS 9.8, unauthenticated auth bypass, KEV due July 17) and CVE-2026-58644 (CVSS 9.8, unauthenticated deserialization RCE, KEV due July 19) are the sharpest edge: no credentials required to reach code execution on SharePoint Server 2016, 2019, and Subscription Edition. CVE-2026-45659 (CVSS 8.8, authenticated deserialization RCE) and CVE-2026-32201 (CVSS 6.5, input validation spoofing) round out the confirmed-exploited set. CVE-2026-55040 (CVSS 9.1, JWT bypass) and CVE-2026-50522 (CVSS 9.8, unauthenticated deserialization) are not yet in KEV but must be patched now. item.title: Microsoft Extractor Suite v3: Release Notes | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Microsoft Extractor Suite v3 lands as the biggest release yet, adding automated M365 and Azure/Entra ID evidence collection, group enumeration, license visibility, and SOF-ELK integration for cloud IR workflows.
Key updates:
- Start-EvidenceCollection is the headline addition: one function kicks off automated acquisition of all Azure/Entra ID and M365 logs, supporting both interactive and automated modes with scope and filtering controls. This is the triage-and-collect workflow cloud responders have needed.
- New enumeration functions fill critical IR gaps: Get-MailboxPermissions maps Full Access, Send As, Send on Behalf, Calendar, and Inbox delegations; Get-Devices inventories all Entra ID registered devices; Get-Groups, Get-GroupMembers, and Get-DynamicGroups expose membership and auto-inclusion rules that attackers abuse for lateral movement and persistence.
- Get-UAL now pulls 180 days by default, retrieves up to 50,000 results via ReturnLargeSet with session IDs, and dynamically calculates optimal retrieval intervals, replacing the fixed 720-minute window. Faster, fewer API calls, less truncated evidence.
- SOF-ELK support added via a -SOF-ELK parameter on UAL acquisition, Get-GraphEntraSignInLogs, and Get-GraphEntraAuditLogs, making ingestion into existing SIEM pipelines cleaner.
Install or update now: Install-Module Microsoft-Extractor-Suite or Update-Module Microsoft-Extractor-Suite.

item.title: Top 5 Windows Events: Essential for Incident Response | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Five Windows Event IDs that Invictus IR reaches for first on real-world incidents, covering lateral movement, persistence, authentication, and log tampering.
Key findings:
- Event ID 1149 (TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager Operational) fires early in an RDP session before authentication completes, making it ideal for hunting lateral movement via nested RDP chains. Combine with 4624 to confirm a full authenticated session and map source IPs and usernames.
- Event ID 4698 (Windows Security) records scheduled task creation, a persistence method favored by Sodinokibi/REvil and IcedID. Check task definitions under Task Scheduler folders and the registry for corroborating artifacts.
- Event ID 4624 (Windows Security) is the authentication anchor: logon type, source, and user in one record. Filter by compromised account to scope lateral movement and detect pass-the-hash (logon type 3 with NTLM).
- Event ID 7045 (Windows System/Security) logs new service installs and is a primary Cobalt Strike indicator. Ransomware groups rely heavily on CS, so this is one of the first checks on any Windows log.
- Event ID 1102 (Windows Security) means the audit log was cleared, almost never legitimate during an incident. Pivot on the user and timestamp; if logs feed a SIEM, the clear event itself becomes an investigation anchor.

item.title: AWS Cloud Native Incident Response: Part 2 | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
AWS Athena is a practical, low-friction triage tool for cloud IR: no indexing required, queries run directly against S3 logs, and cost control is built into how you write queries.
Key details:
- CloudTrail logs stored in S3 are the baseline artifact in most AWS environments. Athena, paired with AWS Glue for schema definition and partitioning, lets responders query them without standing up a SIEM. Glue partitions (region, year, month, day) are critical: queries scoped to a partition scan less data, run faster, and cost less.
- Supported log types for direct Athena loading include CloudTrail, S3 access logs, ELB access logs, VPC Flow Logs, and others with official DDL loading instructions. Each source needs its own DDL statement; the only field to update is the LOCATION pointing to the S3 path.
- Cost discipline matters during IR. Always use LIMIT 10 when exploring an unfamiliar table. Use the query result reuse feature (up to 7 days) when iterating on the same dataset, but disable it when hunting live activity.
- Nested fields require different query approaches. STRUCT fields (like useridentity) are accessible with dot notation. STRING fields like requestparameters require json_extract_scalar, for example: SELECT useridentity.type, json_extract_scalar(requestparameters, '$.roleSessionName') AS roleSessionName FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname = 'AssumeRole' ORDER BY eventtime DESC LIMIT 10.

item.title: Silk Typhoon Threat Profile: Tactics & Defenses | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Silk Typhoon (HAFNIUM), a Chinese 🇨🇳 state APT, has evolved from on-prem Exchange exploitation to cloud-native supply chain attacks, most recently abusing CVE-2025-3928 in Commvault's Azure-hosted M365 backup SaaS to pivot into downstream customer tenants.
- Initial access spans three vectors: CVE-2025-3928 (zero-day in Commvault Web Server, T1190), stolen API keys from privileged cloud vendors (T1195), and leaked corporate credentials found on public repos like GitHub (T1078.004). The Commvault campaign gave them client secrets for Metallic M365 backups, opening direct paths into customer M365 environments via hijacked service principals.
- Lateral movement pivots from on-prem to cloud by targeting Entra Connect servers (T1210, T1078.002), enabling privilege sync between Active Directory and Entra ID. Credential dumping and key vault theft support pass-the-hash moves (T1550.002) into Azure.
- Persistence relies on adding passwords to existing consented service principals or creating new Entra ID applications named to mimic legitimate Office 365 services (T1098.001, T1036). Web shells handle C2 on compromised Azure VMs (T1505.003).
- Collection targets email via EWS and MSGraph APIs, plus SharePoint (T1213.002) and OneDrive (T1213.003), all through OAuth apps with admin consent, a low-noise, API-native exfiltration path that bypasses many endpoint controls.

item.title: Inside wp2shell: How Two WordPress Core Bugs Became a Critical RCE Chain
item.description:
WordPress Core RCE chain "wp2shell" (CVE-2026-63030 + CVE-2026-60137) enables unauthenticated attackers to reach full admin compromise and remote code execution. Emergency patches shipped July 17, 2026.
- CVE-2026-63030 is a REST API auth bypass in WP_REST_Server::serve_batch_request_v1(). Batch requests skip per-request permission checks, letting an unauthenticated caller access protected endpoints. Affects WordPress 6.9.0-6.9.4 and 7.0.0-7.0.1. Fixed in 6.9.5 and 7.0.2.
- CVE-2026-60137 is a SQL injection via the author__not_in parameter in WP_Query. Alone it required auth, limiting real-world risk. Once CVE-2026-63030 removes that barrier, the SQLi becomes reachable from the public internet with no credentials. Affects 6.8.0-6.8.5, 6.9.0-6.9.4, and 7.0.0-7.0.1.
- The chain ends in RCE through WordPress's own admin functionality: malicious plugin upload, theme file edit, or web shell drop. No exotic payload needed after db credentials are cracked offline and admin access is obtained.
- This hits WordPress Core, not a plugin, meaning every unpatched install is exposed regardless of plugin inventory.
Patch first (6.8.6, 6.9.5, or 7.0.2), then assume breach on any exposed instance. Hunt for new admin accounts, PHP files in upload dirs, modified Core files, and anomalous REST API batch requests in web server logs before and after the July 17 disclosure window.

item.title: Cloud IR Infrastructure: Critical Readiness Steps | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Cloud IR readiness across Azure, AWS, and GCP hinges on log centralization and pre-built access paths. Most orgs only start preparing after an incident, and that delay costs critical response time.
- Azure: Centralize Entra Sign-in, Entra Audit, and Azure Activity Logs into Log Analytics. Apply a Delete resource lock on the workspace so a threat actor cannot wipe your evidence. Enable query auditing if insider threat is a concern. Use Conditional Access lockout policies and Privileged Identity Management to contain an active intrusion without fully severing operations.
- AWS: Enable a CloudTrail Org-level trail and store logs in a dedicated archive account with restricted access. Use Athena over S3 to query logs without indexing. Pre-configure an IAM role in the customer org assumable from your IR team's account to cut activation time during a retainer engagement.
- GCP: Enable Log Analytics on logging buckets at creation (cannot be downgraded later). Forward Google Workspace logs to Google Cloud at no cost, making Admin Audit, Login, OAuth Token, and SAML audit logs searchable via SQL in Log Analytics. Pre-assign a Google IAM role to your external IR team's identity at the Org level now.
Takeaway: Run a tabletop against each provider today. Confirm your log pipeline is live, resource locks are set, and IR team access can be activated without depending on the compromised tenant's admin.

item.title: Laundry Bear Threat Profile: Tactics & Defenses | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 state-linked Laundry Bear targets NATO/EU Microsoft 365 environments via stolen cookies, QR phishing, and Evilginx AitM, exfiltrating data from Exchange, SharePoint, and Teams at scale.
Key details:
- Laundry Bear, assessed with high confidence as Russian 🇷🇺 state-affiliated, hit the Dutch 🇳🇱 police in Sept 2024, stealing contact details for ~65,000 officers by purchasing stolen session cookies from criminal marketplaces sourced via infostealer malware, then downloading the Exchange Online Global Address List (GAL) via EWS (T1087, T1539).
- Initial access relies on three paths: pass-the-cookie attacks using purchased credentials (T1078), spearphishing PDFs with malicious QR codes redirecting to typosquatted Entra ID domains (T1566.001), and Evilginx-based AitM to intercept auth tokens mid-session (T1557). Residential proxies (T1090) mask the spraying and C2 traffic.
- Post-access collection hits Exchange Online via EWS/OWA (T1114.002), SharePoint (T1213.002), and Teams (T1213.005). Persistence is maintained by granting delegated email permissions on compromised accounts (T1098).
- Review M365 Unified Audit Log and Entra ID Sign-in Logs for MFA-less logins, anomalous EWS GAL pulls, high-volume mailbox reads, and delegate permission changes. Cross-reference source IPs against residential proxy ranges.
Full TTP table with MITRE ATT&CK mappings is in Invictus IR's GitHub repo.

item.title: Azure Incident Response: 5 Tips to Limit Impact | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Five low-cost Azure hardening controls that directly limit attacker impact and improve forensic readiness, covering identity, billing, logging, and tenant isolation.
Key controls:
- Budget quotas and cost anomaly alerts in Azure Cost Management act as an early tripwire. Attackers spinning up crypto-mining VMs or exfiltrating data generate cost spikes. Navigate to Cost Management and Billing, set a Budget with alert thresholds, then add a Cost Anomaly alert scoped to the subscription. This is a detection layer that costs nothing extra.
- Restricting app registration in Azure AD (User Settings, toggle "Users can register applications" to No) closes a common initial access path. Uncontrolled app registrations have been central to major incidents including SolarWinds and Chinese 🇨🇳 APT campaigns involving OAuth abuse.
- Lock subscription transfers via Azure AD, Subscriptions, Manage Policies, set to "Permit no one." One documented attack pattern involved transferring a subscription to an attacker-controlled tenant while leaving billing on the victim, causing serious financial and access damage.
- Microsoft provides free ingestion for Azure Activity Logs into Log Analytics or Sentinel. These logs capture RunCommands, resource creation, and administrative actions inside a subscription, exactly the evidence you need during IR.

item.title: Microsoft 365 Extractor Suite: Introduction | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Invictus IR releases the Microsoft 365 Extractor Suite, an updated UAL acquisition tool adding MFA support, 100 RecordTypes, and a lightweight mode for faster cloud evidence collection.
- The original Office 365 Extractor lacked MFA support due to how credentials were handled. The new suite uses Connect-ExchangeOnlinePowerShell with modern authentication, supporting both MFA and non-MFA accounts, removing a practical blocker for many investigations.
- RecordType coverage jumps from 76 to 100, meaning more audit event categories pulled from the Unified Audit Log via Search-UnifiedAuditLog. Wider coverage reduces the chance of missing activity across less-common M365 workloads.
- The 5,000-record-per-session API limit is handled by an adaptive interval system. It starts at 480-minute windows and automatically narrows if a window exceeds the cap, making full-month UAL pulls reliable without manual tuning.
- Two scripts ship: Microsoft365_Extractor for full customization, and Microsoft365_Extractor_light for minimal-config acquisition of all logs in a defined period. Run on Windows to avoid known cross-platform errors.
If UAL acquisition is part of your M365 IR playbook, this suite is worth replacing the old Office 365 Extractor. The adaptive interval logic alone makes it more reliable for high-volume tenants. Tool and documentation are on the Invictus IR GitHub.

item.title: The Invisible Architecture of Modern Phishing | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
A 2026 AiTM phishing campaign stitches together ConvertKit, a hijacked Greek 🇬🇷 travel agency site, and JavaScript on Akamai/Linode Object Storage to steal sessions while evading every reputation-based control.
- The lure arrived via ConvertKit, a legitimate email marketing platform, giving it clean SPF/DKIM/DMARC signals. The landing page was a real small business site registered in 2020, a Greek 🇬🇷 travel agency, bypassing domain-age defenses entirely. The threat actor hijacked trust rather than building it.
- Background JavaScript hosted on Akamai and Linode Object Storage acted as the gatekeeper: it pulled the victim's email from the URL, prefilled the login flow for intended targets, and silently redirected everyone else to BestBuy. The proxy logic never lived on the phishing domain itself.
- Blocking the host risks collateral damage to the legitimate business. Blocking the domain is temporary because the attacker can pivot to the next compromised site in minutes. The chain is engineered to outlast standard response playbooks.
- Campaign appears opportunistic, primarily targeting Canada 🇨🇦 and the US 🇺🇸 across construction, agriculture, airport services, and industrial materials. Full IOC list is published on Invictus IR's GitHub.
Treat this as a session theft problem, not a phishing domain problem.

item.title: Stop Using Get-MgAuditLogSignIn: Use These Better Methods | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Get-MgAuditLogSignIn silently drops the Authentication Protocol field, blinding investigators to Device Code phishing logins. Switch to the beta cmdlet or risk missing a key indicator in Entra ID sign-in logs.
- Device Code phishing abuses the OAuth Device Code Flow (T1528) to hijack tokens without capturing credentials. The smoking-gun artifact is the Authentication Protocol field in Entra ID interactive sign-in logs, where the value "Device code flow" identifies the attack. Get-MgAuditLogSignIn and the legacy Get-AzureADAuditSignInLogs both silently omit this field entirely.
- Running Get-Member against Get-MgAuditLogSignIn confirms the field is simply absent from the cmdlet output. The beta replacement, Get-MgBetaAuditLogSignIn, returns nearly double the fields, including Authentication Protocol, Original Transfer Method, and additional Service Principal sign-in details useful for malicious app abuse investigations.
- Two reliable alternatives exist today: the Entra portal filter on Authentication Protocol equals Device Code, or a KQL query against the Entra sign-in logs in Log Analytics targeting the same field. Both surface what the standard cmdlet hides.
- Invictus is updating Microsoft-Extractor-Suite to use the beta cmdlet to close the gap until Microsoft updates the stable module.
If you use Microsoft-Extractor-Suite or raw Get-MgAuditLogSignIn pulls in your IR playbooks, your acquisition is incomplete.

item.title: How to Import Windows Event Logs into Splunk | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Importing offline .evtx files into Splunk requires the preprocess-winevt sourcetype, not wineventlog. Using the wrong sourcetype collapses all events into a single unparseable blob, killing your investigation before it starts.
- The wineventlog sourcetype is designed for live forwarded Windows event logs, not archived .evtx files. Feeding exported binary event logs through it merges everything into one giant event with no field extraction, making searching and timeline reconstruction essentially impossible.
- The correct sourcetype is preprocess-winevt. Set it in inputs.conf alongside your monitor stanza and target path, and Splunk will correctly parse the binary .evtx format, split individual events, and populate fields you can actually query.
- When ingesting a directory of .evtx files using a wildcard monitor path, add crcSalt = to your inputs.conf stanza. Splunk uses a CRC of the first 256 bytes to deduplicate files, and Windows event logs from the same host or time window can share identical headers, causing Splunk to silently skip files you need.
- Splunk must run on Windows Vista, Server 2008, or newer for this to work. If Sysmon logs are in scope, Sysmon must also be installed on the Splunk host for correct parsing of those event types.
For offline DFIR analysis: set sourcetype = preprocess-winevt and crcSalt = in inputs.conf, drop your .evtx files into a watched directory, and Splunk will ingest the full event set ready for timeline and TTP hunting.

item.title: Master Entra ID Identity Protection: The Ultimate IR Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Microsoft Entra ID Identity Protection's four risky reports are underused during IR. Here is how to read them, extract them, and avoid the containment traps that leave attackers active.
Key findings:
- The four reports: Risky Users, Risky Workload Identities, Risky Sign-ins, and Risk Detections have different retention windows. Risky Sign-ins covers only 30 days; Risk Detections extends to 90. During triage, go to Risk Detections first so you do not miss early-stage activity that has already aged out of the sign-in report.
- Containment actions have silent failure modes. "Confirm user compromised" only elevates risk to High; without a Conditional Access policy acting on High risk, nothing is blocked and no session is killed. "Confirm user safe" removes the risk flag and feeds negative feedback to Microsoft, which can suppress future detections if an attacker triggers it.
- Workload identities (service principals, managed identities) are flagged separately and are frequently missed. Microsoft detects leaked credentials, anomalous activity, and admin-confirmed compromise for these accounts, but most IR tooling does not surface them by default.
- For extraction, use the Microsoft Extractor Suite: Install-Module -Name Microsoft-Extractor-Suite, then Get-RiskyUsers and Get-RiskyDetections. Risky Sign-ins come through the standard Entra Sign-in log pull. Risky Workload Identities extraction is listed as work in progress.

item.title: Nebius Cloud Incident Response: Part 1 (Neocloud) | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Nebius Neocloud IR fundamentals: IAM blind spots, audit log gaps, and a free acquisition script for responders working AI-first GPU cloud environments.
Key findings:
- Nebius organizes resources in Tenant/Project hierarchy. The Tenant ID (format: tenant-e00mzw6m41jbhs75m6) defines blast radius. A compromised project does not automatically mean tenant-wide exposure, so scope early by pulling both Tenant ID and Name before taking containment action.
- Federated users are the critical IAM blind spot. Nebius only logs the successful token, not the auth attempt. Brute force, impossible travel, and MFA fatigue artifacts live exclusively in your external IdP (Entra Sign-in logs). In a federated environment, pivot out of Nebius immediately.
- Audit logs use CloudEvents JSON format, accessible via GUI or CLI (nebius audit v2 audit-event). Key IR fields: .time (timeline), .type (e.g. accesskey.create), .subject (actor), .resource (target). Data Plane logs, which show file access and source IP, are in preview and off by default. Most orgs will not have them. Retention appears to be 90 days, undocumented.
- Top threat vectors mapped to ATT&CK: Cryptojacking/GPU hijacking (T1496), model exfiltration (AML.T0010), data poisoning (AML.T0020), supply chain via Hugging Face or Docker Hub (T1195), and agentic prompt injection abuse (AML.T0051).
Use the Invictus-Nebius script to dump 90 days of audit logs across all accessible tenants into JSON.

item.title: Sea Turtle Threat Profile: Tactics & Defenses | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Sea Turtle, a Türkiye-nexus espionage actor, has pivoted from DNS hijacking to cloud-focused intrusions, exploiting stolen IAM credentials and a zero-day to target government, telco, and tech sector cloud environments.
Key findings:
- Sea Turtle (a.k.a. Cosmic Wolf) used stolen AWS IAM keys or Azure Entra ID credentials (T1078.004) to authenticate, then executed malicious commands via AWS CLI or Azure CLI/PowerShell (T1059.009) to interact with EC2, S3, IAM, VMs, and Blob storage. No malware required at the cloud layer.
- Persistence came through security group modification (T1543.005/T1578): the actor opened TCP/22 from attacker-controlled IPs, then used SSH as both a C2 channel (T1071) and exfiltration path (T1041), blending with legitimate admin activity.
- Since April 2024, the group has been exploiting CVE-2025-27920, a zero-day in Output Messenger, targeting unpatched user accounts as an initial access vector before pivoting to cloud environments.
- Key forensic sources: AWS CloudTrail management and data events, Azure Activity Log, NSG and VPC Flow Logs for unexpected TCP/22 connections, and Entra ID sign-in logs for credentials used from non-organization IPs.
Hunt CloudTrail and Azure Activity Log for CLI-sourced API calls from unknown IPs, security group rule changes opening port 22, and IAM keys or service principals older than 60 days with external-source logins.

item.title: Automated AWS Incident Response: New Capabilities | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Invictus-AWS gets a major update with automated CloudTrail analysis via Athena, multi-region acquisition, and modular step execution, giving AWS responders a faster path from log collection to triage.
Key details:
- The centrepiece addition is automated CloudTrail log analysis using roughly 25 predefined Athena SQL queries stored in queries.yaml. Point the tool at an S3 bucket of CloudTrail logs and it runs the query set, surfacing hits to terminal and file output without manual query writing.
- Multi-region support is now native. Run against a single region (-r eu-west-3) or sweep all activated regions in the account (-A), optionally seeding a priority region first. Previous versions were single-region only, a real gap in environments with sprawling footprints.
- Execution is now modular across four independent steps: service enumeration, configuration collection, log acquisition, and log analysis (-s 1,2 or -s 4). Steps no longer fail together, and responders can re-run only what they need, useful mid-investigation when you already have logs collected.
- Output flexibility now includes local storage alongside the default S3 write (-w local), creating a results folder per region. API pagination is also fixed: earlier versions capped AWS API responses at 100 results, which silently undercounted resources in large environments.
Takeaway: if your AWS IR workflow still relies on manual Athena queries or single-region collection, this update closes both gaps.

item.title: AWS Incident Response: Responding to Attacks | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Exposed S3 credentials file led to full AWS compromise: lateral movement, new IAM user creation, database theft, and ~200MB exfiltrated. S3 access logs and AWS billing filled gaps where CloudTrail went silent.
Key findings:
- Initial access traced via S3 access logs, not CloudTrail. One minute before the first malicious console login at 21:23:20 UTC on 26-10-2022, attacker IP 185.195.232[.]111 performed a GET request (HTTP 200) against a publicly accessible S3 bucket containing a plaintext credentials file. That file handed over the DevOps1-bpvbp account. CloudTrail alone would have missed this entirely.
- Post-access activity (T1136, T1537): attacker created rogue IAM user DevOps3, used Session Manager to pivot into EC2 instance i-08e56d6b6c0439daf, created S3 bucket eu-west-1-prod-data in eu-west-1, and copied staff.txt to it via "aws s3 cp".
- CloudTrail object-level data events were not enabled on the attacker-created bucket, making S3 server access logs and billing data the only remaining sources. item.description:

item.title: macOS Incident Response: Part 1 Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
macOS IR Part 1: Invictus maps MITRE ATT&CK execution techniques to concrete artifacts, covering AppleScript, Unix shell history, cron jobs, and launchctl across real malware cases.
Key findings:
- AppleScript (T1059) is a persistent attacker tool: it can be compiled "run-only" with no recoverable source, executed silently via the osascript binary, or packaged as a signed app. SentinelOne's AEVT tool is the current option for reverse engineering compiled scripts.
- Shell history is a high-value artifact but fragile. Pull full zsh history with timestamps using "history -df 0" and inspect ~/.zsh_sessions for session files with restoration timestamps. Note: history is trivially wiped, so corroborate with other sources.
- Cron and "at" jobs leave execution evidence in /usr/lib/cron/jobs, including the command run and its output. The Janicab malware used cron to schedule tasks and store scripts in a hidden directory. "at -l" gives execution timestamps for timeline correlation.
- Launchctl is dual-purpose: one-time execution and persistence. Calisto Trojan used "launchctl list com.apple.screensharing" to enable screen sharing silently. LoudMiner used it to suppress QEMU if Activity Monitor was detected.
Hunt: on any macOS triage, pull zsh and bash history with timestamps, enumerate /usr/lib/cron/jobs, and list all launchctl-managed agents and daemons. MITRE ATT&CK layer and mindmap for the full series are on Invictus IR's GitHub.

item.title: Cobalt Strike Response Guide: Part 3 | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
In-memory Cobalt Strike leaves almost no disk artifacts, making memory forensics the primary recovery path. This guide covers full image analysis with Volatility and process dump parsing to extract beacon configs.
Key details:
- Cobalt Strike is commonly injected into legitimate Windows processes like svchost.exe via PowerShell to avoid disk-based detection (T1055). The tell is svchost making unexpected external connections, visible via Volatility's netscan plugin.
- For full memory images, three Volatility plugins do the heavy lifting: psscan to find hidden or terminated processes, pstree to map parent/child relationships and spot anomalies, and cmdscan to surface the command line used to launch each process. Suspicious PowerShell command lines are a key artifact.
- malfind identifies injected code or DLLs by examining VAD tags and page permissions. It flags candidates for deeper analysis rather than confirming infection outright.
- JPCERT's cobaltstrikescan and cobaltstrikeconfig Volatility plugins extract Cobalt Strike beacon configs directly from memory. Note: these only work with Volatility 2.x.
- When a full image is unavailable, dump the target process using Task Manager or Process Hacker and parse it with the SentinelOne Cobalt Strike parser to pull C2 configuration and IOCs without manual debugger analysis.
If svchost or other system processes show outbound connections in netscan, dump and parse immediately.

item.title: MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs: The Complete Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs closes a critical blind spot in Microsoft 365 IR: Graph API calls by Entra ID apps were largely unaudited, a gap exploited in Storm-0558 and SolarWinds.
Key findings:
- The MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs table in Log Analytics captures every HTTP request the Graph API received and processed for a tenant. Key fields include AppId, UserId, ServicePrincipalId, RequestUri, RequestMethod, ResponseStatusCode, ResponseSizeBytes, IpAddress, UserAgent, Scopes, and Roles. Requires a P1 or P2 Entra ID license and must be enabled via Diagnostic Settings.

- Correlate Graph API hits against Entra ID Audit Logs. A Graph request to create a user will not be self-contained in this table alone. Cross-referencing is required to confirm execution and recover user details.
- Practical limits: the log is extremely noisy (all requests, all apps, no granular filtering), and storage costs in Log Analytics or a Storage Account will be significant. No data reduction options exist yet beyond full on/off.

item.title: Azure Incident Response: Complete Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Azure cross-tenant synchronization (CTS) can be weaponized for stealthy persistence, letting an attacker inject users from a controlled tenant into a victim tenant with minimal noise.
Key findings:
- The attack requires the Hybrid Administrator role in the victim tenant. Once configured, the attacker adds their tenant as a trusted partner, enabling automatic user provisioning into the victim environment. The critical audit log event to hunt is "Add a partner to cross-tenant access setting," which captures the attacker's tenant ID and the initiating user's UPN.
- The Audit Log is the only reliable source. Sign-in logs, Provisioning logs, and the Activity log do not record CTS setup. Portal-generated consent pop-ups leave no log trace at all, so GUI-only actions are silent.
- Synchronized users arrive tagged as ExternalAzureAD and B2B, but B2B alone does not confirm CTS abuse. Correlation with the initial "Add a partner" audit event is the only way to distinguish CTS-provisioned accounts from ordinary guest invitations.
- Microsoft records a proxy IP from their own range on the victim side, not the attacker's real source IP. The actual source IP only appears in audit logs on the attacker-controlled tenant, which responders typically cannot access.
Takeaway: Run this KQL against AuditLogs in Microsoft Sentinel: filter OperationName == "Add a partner to cross-tenant access setting," extract initiating_user, source_ip, and target_tenant.

item.title: Daxin: 13-Year-Old China-Linked Malware Found Still Active on Manufacturer’s Network
item.description:
Chinese-linked Daxin rootkit, first documented in 2022 with roots to 2013, found still running in 2026 on a Taiwanese 🇹🇼 manufacturer's network alongside a previously unknown backdoor called Stupig.
- Daxin is a Windows kernel-mode driver that never makes outbound C2 connections. Instead it monitors incoming TCP traffic for specific patterns and hijacks existing legitimate connections to carry encrypted C2 traffic, making it invisible to tools hunting for suspicious outbound destinations. Multi-hop routing lets operators reach air-gapped hosts through a chain of compromised machines.
- Stupig (kbdus1.dll) persists by registering as a keyboard-layout provider, causing win32k.sys to load it into winlogon.exe at boot. It intercepts usernames prefixed with "stupig" at the login screen and executes the remainder as SYSTEM, before any user authenticates and without generating a logon audit event.
- Both artifacts carry 2013 compile timestamps. Telemetry only appeared May 12, 2026, implying up to 13 years of undetected access. Suspected initial access was a Digiwin SSO portal running end-of-life JDK 1.5/1.6.
Takeaway: Hunt for unsigned or unexpected DLLs loaded into winlogon.exe, and audit keyboard-layout provider registrations in HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Keyboard Layouts. Full report from Symantec's Threat Hunter Team contains additional details.

item.title: From SQL Injection to Infrastructure-Level RCE: A PostgreSQL Superuser Compromise
item.description:
SQL injection in a government financial portal escalates to unauthenticated RCE via PostgreSQL superuser access, exposing employee PII and full infrastructure control.
- The entry point was pJobNumber in vss00CvStatusData.php, a parameter concatenated directly into a SQL query with no parameterization. A single quote triggered a raw PostgreSQL error, confirming classic error-based SQLi (T1190). UNION SELECT with NULL placeholders revealed a three-column query structure, enabling clean data extraction.
- The web app connected to the database as the native postgres superuser account. That single misconfiguration collapsed every privilege boundary: no escalation needed, the attacker landed with full database control from the first successful injection.
- With superuser access, PostgreSQL system catalogs were wide open. The auditor enumerated public.vss01tpemployee and found employee names, PAN numbers, and financial records. From there, PostgreSQL's COPY TO/FROM and pg_read_file or PROGRAM extensions make OS-level RCE a short step.
- The portal belongs to state financial infrastructure (vsswb). Full unauthenticated RCE on a government network via a single unparameterized parameter is a critical-severity finding, and the disclosed bureaucratic non-response is a reminder that responsible disclosure does not always close the loop.
If you audit web apps backed by PostgreSQL, confirm the DB user in query responses.

item.description:

item.title: Case Study: The DangerDev@protonmail.me Investigation | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
An exposed AWS IAM access key with AdministratorAccess led to a month-long intrusion: cryptomining, SES-based phishing, fake PayPal domains, and a cross-account backdoor role the defenders almost missed.

item.title: You Assume Your Logs Are Flowing.
item.description:
Silent log pipeline failures in Microsoft Sentinel create blind spots that look identical to a quiet, healthy SOC, across four distinct failure points that standard health checks miss.

The Heartbeat table query with a reliability filter (active 5 of 7 days minimum) surfaces machines that went silent, while a day-over-day Usage table comparison flags tables that dropped volume by 20-100% or went completely dark. Status labels like "TABLE WENT SILENT" and "CRITICAL DROP" give responders immediate triage priority.
- DCR transformation errors drop rows silently. Enabling error logging per Data Collection Rule exposes these via DCRLogErrors. The Operation table catches workspace-level rejections such as exceeding the 500-column limit on custom tables or V2 custom log schema mismatches. SentinelHealth reveals connector fetch failures (401s, 429s, timeouts) that never reach the DCR layer at all, meaning everything upstream looks healthy while no data is flowing.
- Data can land in the wrong table. Windows Security Events routed to the generic Event table instead of SecurityEvent still get ingested and billed, but detections miss them entirely. A SentinelHealth query comparing DestinationTable to StreamName where they do not match surfaces this misconfiguration.
- Ingestion lag kills near-real-time rules silently.

item.title: Confused Deputy: Google IdP Universal Account Takeover via Device Code Flow Hijacking
item.description:
Two stacked bugs in Google's OAuth device code flow (RFC 8628) enabled silent, one-click account takeover on any "Sign in with Google" app, including Gmail via IMAP, with no consent screen and no 2FA prompt.
Key findings:
- Bug 1: Google's device-code sign-in session is transferable via URL. The challenge endpoint at accounts.google[.]com/v3/signin/challenge carries an encrypted blob (TL=) anchoring the device poll. - Bug 2: client_id and scope are never server-side validated against the issued device_code. Swapping YouTube TV's client_id for Google Cloud SDK's, with scope=cloud-platform,compute,appengine.admin, caused the token poll to return elevated cloud tokens, not YouTube tokens.

- Gmail IMAP access was achievable via XOAUTH2 on imap.gmail[.]com:993 using the substituted token after the Gmail REST API blocked it at the project layer. Full inbox access confirmed.

item.title: How I Detected an Insider Threat in Splunk When Every Single Action Looked Legitimate
item.description:
Insider threat caught in Splunk: three individually legitimate Windows events correlated into a confirmed PII exfiltration, with no exploit, no failed auth, and no perimeter alert firing.
Key findings:
- The kill chain: Event ID 4663 (file read on C:\CustomerExports\payments_export.csv), Event ID 4104 (PowerShell Compress-Archive via Script Block Logging), and Event ID 5156 (curl.exe outbound on port 4444) each looked clean in isolation. - None of these log by default. File System auditing plus a SACL, PowerShell Script Block Logging, and Filtering Platform Connection must be explicitly enabled. If they are off when the attack runs, the evidence was never written.

Triage immediately: isolate the host, disable (do not delete) the account, pull all files touched in that session window, and hand a clean timeline to IR and HR jointly. Full SPL and lab at github[.]com/ronakmishra28/meridian-soc-detection-lab.

item.title: Investigating Persistence Mechanisms in AWS

The trail is in CloudTrail: filter requestParameters.userName for unknown accounts, exclude Get/List/Describe noise, and group by userIdentity.arn plus eventName to surface what permissions were granted and by whom.
- iam:CreateRole or iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy with external account IDs in the Principal block gives attacker-controlled accounts cross-account assume-role access. Hunt CloudTrail for CreateRole and UpdateAssumeRolePolicy events whose policyDocument contains unrecognized account IDs, then pull all sts:AssumeRole calls from those accounts.
- Lambda backdoors (T1059) deploy Python that calls iam:CreateUser, attaches AdministratorAccess, and returns plaintext credentials.
